About Diwali: frequently asked questions What is Diwali in simple words? Diwali is the Hindu festival of lights, celebrated each autumn on the new-moon night of the month of Kartika. People light rows of oil lamps, decorate their homes with rangoli, worship Goddess Lakshmi for prosperity, wear new clothes, share sweets and set off fireworks to celebrate the victory of light over darkness and good over evil. What does the word Diwali mean? Diwali is short for Deepavali, a Sanskrit word made of deepa, meaning lamp or light, and avali, meaning a row or series. Deepavali therefore means a row of lamps, after the lines of clay diyas lit on the festival night. Why is Diwali called the festival of lights? Diwali is called the festival of lights because lamps are its central symbol. It falls on Amavasya, the darkest night of the month, and homes, temples and streets are lit with rows of diyas, candles and lanterns to drive away the darkness. passages.text: What is Diwali? The word Diwali means ârows of lighted lampsâ. It is celebrated by Hindu people across the world. Diwali is known as the âfestival of lightsâ because houses, shops and public places are decorated with small oil lamps called âdiyasâ. Diwali is also celebrated in Sikhism and Jainism. Diwali always falls some time between October and November, but the exact date varies each year as the Hindu calendar is based on the Moon. In 2026, Diwali is on Sunday 8 November. The story of Diwali 1 of 10 How is Diwali celebrated? For many people this five day festival honours Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth. Lamps are lit and windows and doors are left open to help Lakshmi find her way into people's homes. Other ways that Hindus celebrate the festival include: - Spring-cleaning the home - Wearing new clothes - Exchanging gifts (often sweets and dried fruits) and preparing festive meals - Decorating buildings with fancy lights - Huge fireworks displays Thinking points Have a look at the thinking points below. The main night is the Amavasya (new moon) of Kartika in the purnimanta calendar used in North India, the same night that the amanta calendar used in much of West and South India calls the Amavasya of Ashvin. Diwali usually comes about 20 days after Dussehra. Lakshmi Puja is held when the Amavasya tithi is present in the evening after sunset, which is why the festival sometimes shifts by a day from what a simple calendar would suggest. In 2026 Diwali is on Sunday, 8 November, with Dhanteras on Friday, 6 November and Bhai Dooj on Wednesday, 11 November. See all five days and future Diwali dates in the Diwali 2026 guide. Diwali around the world The main day of Diwali is an official public holiday in India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Malaysia (except Sarawak), Singapore, Mauritius, Fiji, Guyana, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago and Pakistan. The word Diwali is a shortened form of the Sanskrit Deepavali. It joins two words: deepa, meaning a lamp or light, and avali, meaning a row or series. Deepavali therefore means "a row of lamps", a name that describes the festival exactly, since lines of small clay lamps are lit along doorsteps, windows, walls and riverbanks. The form Deepavali is still used in South India, Sri Lanka, Malaysia and Singapore, while Diwali is more common in North India and abroad. Why is Diwali called the festival of lights? Diwali falls on Amavasya, the darkest night of the lunar month, and its central act is lighting that darkness. It coincides with the day of Kali Chaudas. It is believed that spirits roam around on the night of Kali Chaudas, and Hanuman, who is the deity of strength, power, and protection, is worshipped to seek protection from the spirits. Diwali is also celebrated to mark the return of Rama to Ayodhya after defeating the demon-king Ravana[132] and completing his fourteen years of exile. The devotion and dedication of Hanuman pleased Rama so much that he blessed Hanuman to be worshipped before him. Thus, people worship Hanuman the day before Diwali's main day.[133] This day is commonly celebrated as Diwali in Tamil Nadu, Goa, and Karnataka.[citation needed] Traditionally, Marathi Hindus and South Indian Hindus receive an oil massage from the elders in the family on the day and then take a ritual bath, all before sunrise.[134] Many visit their favourite Hindu temple.[135]

Diwali is shared by four faiths, each with its own reason for lighting lamps on the same night. - Hindus celebrate Rama's return to Ayodhya, Krishna's victory over the demon Narakasura, and the worship of Goddess Lakshmi; in Bengal, Assam and Odisha the night is given to Goddess Kali. - Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, the day Guru Hargobind was released from Gwalior Fort and returned to Amritsar, where the Golden Temple is lit up. - Jains mark the day Lord Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara, attained nirvana at Pawapuri in Bihar, with lamps, prayers and fasting. - Newar Buddhists in Nepal celebrate Swanti, their version of Tihar, including Mha Puja, the "worship of the self", which also marks the Nepal Sambat New Year. In India, Diwali has also become a national festival enjoyed by people of every background. To see how its customs differ from state to state, read Diwali celebrations in India. The light carries several meanings at once: - Good over evil: the lamps celebrate victories of good, above all Rama's return after defeating Ravana. - Knowledge over ignorance: in Hindu thought, light stands for knowledge and the inner self, and the lamp is a reminder to dispel ignorance within. - Welcoming prosperity: lit, clean homes are believed to draw Goddess Lakshmi, who brings wealth and good fortune. - A fresh start: for many communities Diwali begins a new financial or calendar year, so the light marks a new beginning. The story most often told about the first Diwali is that the people of Ayodhya lit rows of lamps to welcome Lord Rama, Sita and Lakshmana home after 14 years of exile.
